title: Fights at dances, and a policeman in Dallas
summary: Few fights at New Orleans dances versus knife-checking in Dallas; a Dallas policeman stopped Albert with his trumpet.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Did you have many humbugs on the job where you were playing? I mean like in the audience? Fights? Yeah, fights and stuff.

Not that I can ever recall. The dances started early and they cut out early. But I can't ever recall. There might have been some differences there, but not no major fights as I said before. I can't recall. And Texas was a little different. They did have places there where it was always a knockout drag out.

In Texas. When I first went to Dallas, there was a place where I played upstairs. They had a man on the door to search each customer to come up. They had a bucket there on the side to drop the knives and the pistols in until they come out. But I never recall seeing anything like that in New Orleans. And I'll play to some tremendous crowds here. At the old Santa Center Club when I played there. I remember 1500, man. In those days, 1500 is equal to 5,000, 6,000, 7,000, 8,000 a day. And I can't recall any arguments or fights. Of course, a lot of times the audience was confined to the bandstand watching the band play. And they would just hang around and leave when the dancers are out. No trouble. But today, you can't tell when trouble is going to happen. I've never witnessed too much of it here yet because I guess it's maybe because I don't live here and I don't get a chance to go to these things. But I do read in Louisiana, Rita, about a lot of murders and things that go on here that are not associated with entertainment.
Well, yeah. That can happen anywhere. Right. On the street. Right.
Just be walking home at night. That's right. Well, that's predominant over the United States today. Yeah. So it's not confined to one city only.
Were you ever afraid walking home at night in any neighborhood?

I'll tell you, the first time that I, when I left New Orleans and I went to Dallas, Texas, I was so happy to be going away from New Orleans on my, starting on my career. I was always loved my family. So I was going on to the Western Union, which was about four, six or seven blocks from where I was playing. I was on the main street to Dallas. And I had a brand new trumpet. So I went into the Western Union and I said, no mother, telegram. And told her everything was all right and this, that, and the other. So when I came out, the policeman stopped me and says, what do you got in that box? Well, I'm about 60 years old. And I'm used to the lights in New Orleans staying all night, traveling the streets all night. They surprised me. I said, well, I got a trumpet. He said, open it. Now what he was looking for, I don't know, but after going through all these different things, these different phases in my life, maybe he was looking for don't. So he said, what else you have? And I said, nothing. So I said, I'm a musician. I just finished playing. He said, well, you're in a bad neighborhood. You see? It's on the main street.
